title: 10 Money Mistakes to Avoid in Your 20s (and How to Fix Each)
description: Ten money mistakes to avoid in your 20s, with the real cost of each one worked out in numbers and the smallest fix you can start in under an hour.

takeaways: Most money mistakes in your 20s come from not looking: at your spending, at interest rates, at what you are paid.
Paying only the minimum on a $2,000 card balance at 22% can take over 11 years and cost about $2,600 in interest.
Each mistake has a small fix you can start in under an hour. Starting imperfectly now beats starting properly in five years.
body:
Your 20s are when most people get their first real income and their first real bills, with almost no instruction on either. The mistakes below are common because nobody teaches the alternative.

None of them is permanent. Each one has a fix that takes less than an hour to start, and where it helps, the cost is worked out in numbers so you can see what is at stake.

## 1. Not knowing where the money goes

Plenty of people can tell you their salary and can't tell you what they spent on food last month. Without that, every other money decision is a guess.

**Fix:** open last month's statement and add up five lines: housing, food, transport, subscriptions, everything else. It takes thirty minutes and it is the base of [a simple budget](/blog/budget-on-less-than-1000-a-month/).

## 2. Letting spending rise with every raise

More income arrives, and the nicer flat, newer phone and takeaway habit arrive with it. You earn more and feel just as broke. People call this lifestyle creep.

**Fix:** when your pay goes up, send half of the increase to savings or debt from the first month. If you get $200 more, $100 moves automatically and $100 is yours to enjoy. You still get an upgrade, and you keep part of the raise.

## 3. Having no emergency cushion

One repair or one short pay cheque and the credit card comes out. Then the interest makes next month tighter.

This is very common. In the Federal Reserve's latest household survey, more than a third of US adults said they couldn't cover a $400 surprise with cash.

**Fix:** open a separate account and build a small starter fund. Here is [how to build an emergency fund on a low income](/blog/emergency-fund-on-a-small-income/).

## 4. Paying only the minimum on a credit card

The minimum payment is designed to keep you in debt for as long as possible. Here is what that looks like.

Take a $2,000 balance at 22% interest, which is close to the current average rate on US cards that carry a balance. Assume a typical minimum of 1% of the balance plus that month's interest, with a $25 floor.

| How you pay | Time to clear | Interest paid |
|---|---|---:|
| Minimum only | 139 months (over 11 years) | About $2,600 |
| Fixed $60 a month | 52 months | About $1,119 |
| Fixed $100 a month | 26 months | About $514 |

On the minimum, you pay back more in interest than you borrowed. A fixed $100 a month clears it in just over two years.

Card issuers calculate minimums in slightly different ways, so your figures will vary. The pattern won't.

**Fix:** pay a fixed amount above the minimum and choose an order for your debts. The two main methods are compared with real numbers in [debt snowball vs avalanche](/blog/debt-snowball-vs-avalanche/).

## 5. Signing up for payments you haven't added up

A phone contract. A gym. Three streaming services. Two buy-now-pay-later plans. Each looks small on its own.

Four "pay in four" purchases at $37.50 a fortnight each is $150 leaving your account every two weeks, often on different days, which makes it hard to notice.

**Fix:** list every fixed monthly payment and total it. If the number surprises you, cancel the one you'd miss least.

## 6. Waiting to save until you earn more

Saving $50 feels pointless. It isn't, and the reason is time.

Put $50 a month away for 40 years at an average 6% annual return and you end up with about $99,600, having paid in $24,000. Start ten years later and save for 30 years, and you get about $50,200. Waiting a decade cuts the result roughly in half.

The 6% is an assumption used to show how growth compounds, not a prediction. Returns are never guaranteed and they vary from year to year.

**Fix:** set up an automatic transfer for an amount so small it feels slightly embarrassing. Raise it when you can.

## 7. Never asking for more

Many people accept the first salary they are offered and never negotiate a raise, a rate or a bill. Over a career, that silence gets expensive.

**Fix:** before your next review or job offer, look up what the role pays elsewhere and ask for a specific number. For bills such as phone and internet, one call a year asking for a better deal is often enough.

## 8. Not building a skill that raises your income

Cutting costs has a floor. You can't spend less than zero. Income doesn't have the same ceiling.

Your 20s are the cheapest time to learn something that pays, because you usually have more time than obligations.

**Fix:** pick one skill and give it a few hours a week for three months. Here are the [best online skills to learn for income](/blog/best-online-skills-to-learn-for-income/). If you want to earn while you learn, try one of these [side hustles that cost nothing to start](/blog/side-hustles-for-students-zero-investment/).

## 9. Lending money you can't afford to lose

Helping friends and family is part of life in many families and cultures, and that is a good thing. The mistake is lending your rent money and then not being able to pay your own rent.

**Fix:** decide in advance how much you can give without hurting yourself, and treat it as a gift. If it comes back, good.

## 10. Avoiding the subject because it is stressful

Unopened letters. Unchecked balances. Unanswered emails from a lender. Avoiding it feels better today and makes every problem bigger.

**Fix:** set a fixed fifteen-minute slot each week to look at your accounts. Nothing else, only looking. Most money problems are less frightening once you can see their size.

## Which mistake costs the most?

For most people it is number 4, because credit card interest compounds against you every month. Number 6 is the most expensive over a lifetime, but you don't feel it until much later, which is exactly why it is easy to ignore.

## Where to start

Don't try to fix all ten. Start with number 1, because knowing your numbers makes the other nine easier to judge. Then pick whichever one is costing you the most right now.

If you have already made several of these, so has nearly everyone. A mistake at 23 costs little compared with the same mistake repeated until 40. Stopping it now is the whole win.
